fullPassage: Have you ever felt bored, even though you were busy and successful? In his book The Big Leap, Gay Hendricks presents a framework that divides the activities in our lives into four zones. The first is the Zone of Incompetence: things we are simply not good at. They can frustrate and exhaust us. The second is the Zone of Competence: things we can do well enough, but many other people could do just as well. These activities may not be especially exciting or satisfying. The third is the Zone of Excellence, where many successful people spend much of their time. These are skills we have mastered, and we are often rewarded and praised for them. Yet Hendricks calls this zone "a trap." We may look successful on the outside, but we can feel empty or exhausted on the inside. Because this zone feels safe and rewarding, it can be difficult to leave. The fourth is the Zone of Genius: the unique place where our special abilities, what we love to do, and the value we create come together. In this zone, we may feel deeply engaged in what we are doing. Time can seem to fly, and even hard work may feel almost effortless. Hendricks also describes the Upper Limit Problem. He suggests that people sometimes create problems for themselves when they begin to experience more happiness or success than they are comfortable with. They may worry, procrastinate, or even start conflicts without fully realizing why. He sees this resistance as a sign that we may be approaching a personal limit on how much success or happiness we are comfortable with. So how can we spend more time in our Zone of Genius? Hendricks suggests starting with just ten minutes a day and gradually giving more time to activities in this zone. In The Big Leap, he describes spending 70 percent or more of his time in his Zone of Genius as a possible long-term goal. The idea is to begin with a small step and gradually make more room for activities that use our strengths and give us energy.

questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

❌ ③ spend: 'many successful people spend much of their time' — 복수 주어에 맞춘 동사로 정상

questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

❌ ③ what: 'what we love to do' — 선행사를 포함한 관계대명사('~하는 것')로 정상

questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?

det.korean: 겉은 성공적이지만 속은 '공허하거나(empty)' 탈진할 수 있음. content(만족한)는 부적절

❌ ② satisfying — 원문 일치. 역량의 영역의 일은 특별히 '만족스럽지' 않을 수 있다는 맥락에 적절

✅ ③ content — 원문은 empty(공허한). 'but(그러나)'이 겉(성공적으로 보임)과 속의 대비를 이끄므로 속은 '공허하거나 탈진한' 상태여야 한다. content(만족한)는 겉과 같은 방향이라 대비가 무너지고, 이 영역을 '덫'이라 부른 이유도 사라짐 ← 정답

❌ ④ energy — 원문 일치. 강점을 쓰는 활동이 '에너지'를 준다는 결론에 적절
det.tip: look successful on the outside, BUT feel empty on the inside — but 앞뒤는 반대 방향

questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

In his book The Big Leap, Gay Hendricks presents a framework that divides the activities in our lives into four zones. The first is the Zone of Incompetence: things we are simply not good at. They can frustrate and exhaust us. The second is the Zone of Competence: things we can do well enough, but many other people could do just as well. These activities may not be especially exciting or satisfying. The third is the Zone of Excellence, where many successful people spend much of their time. These are skills we have mastered, and we are often rewarded and praised for them. Yet Hendricks calls this zone "a trap." We may look successful on the outside, but we can feel empty or exhausted on the inside. Because this zone feels safe and rewarding, it can be difficult to leave. The fourth is the Zone of Genius: the unique place where our special abilities, what we love to do, and the value we create come together. In this zone, we may feel deeply engaged in what we are doing. Time can seem to fly, and even hard work may feel almost effortless. Hendricks also describes the Upper Limit Problem. He suggests that people sometimes create problems for themselves when they begin to experience more happiness or success than they are comfortable with. They may worry, procrastinate, or even start conflicts without fully realizing why. He sees this resistance as a sign that we may be approaching a personal limit on how much success or happiness we are comfortable with. So how can we spend more time in our Zone of Genius? Hendricks suggests starting with just ten minutes a day and gradually giving more time to activities in this zone. In The Big Leap, he describes spending 70 percent or more of his time in his Zone of Genius as a possible long-term goal. The idea is to begin with a small step and gradually make more room for activities that use our strengths and give us energy.
